full_judgment:
This revisional application under section 439 read with section 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been preferred for setting aside the judgment and order dated 28-3-95 passed by the Additional District Magistrate, Madaripur in Criminal Appeal No. 37 of 1992 dismissing the appeal by affirming the judgment and order dated 3-6-92 passed by the Additional District Magistrate, Madaripur in GR Case No. 16 of 1991 convicting the accused-petitioner No. 1 Moslem Mollah alias Fattah Mollah under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code and sentencing him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3(three) years and to pay a fine of Taka 500.00 in default to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months more, convicting the accused petitioner Nos.2-4 namely, 2. Mojlem Akon, 3. Shahjahan Khan, 4. Ayub Ali Howlader alias Abub Ali under section 326 of the Penal Code and sentencing each of them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3(three) years and to pay a fine of Taka 500 each in default to suffer simple imprisonment for 6 (six) months more, convicting the accused-petitioner No. 5 Shaheb All Howlader alias Shaheb Ali under section 323 of the Penal Code and sentencing him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1 year. 

 4. Mr. Khondaker Mahbub Hossain, the learned Senior Advocate along with Mr. Golam Kibria, the learned Advocate appeared for the accused-petitioners and Mr. MA Hafiz, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the State. The learned Advocate appearing for the accused petitioners submits that the accused Moslem Ali Mollah alias Fattah Mollah was charged under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code on the allegations as under: 

 5. He then submitted that there is no evidence on record to show that on the order of this accused-petitioner any injury was caused to the informant Habibur Rahman by any of the accused persons and, as such, the order of conviction and sentence tinder sections 326/114 of the Penal Code against him is liable to be set aside. He further submitted that the accused-petitioner Shahajahan Khan has been convicted; that the accused-petitioner Shahjahan Khan has been convicted and sentenced under section 326 of the Penal Code for causing injuries to the father of the informant but from the evidence of the Medical Officer PW 8 Dr. Md. Matiur Rahman it is clear that the injuries on the person of victim Sk. Md. Chand Mia are simple in nature. So the conviction under section 326 of the Penal Code is also bad in law and accordingly, liable to be set aside. He then argued that accused-petitioner Ayub Ali was convicted under section 326 of the Penal Code for allegedly causing injuries to PW Mosharaf Hossain and from the evidence of PW 8 Dr. Md. Matiur Rahman it appear that the injuries on the person of PW Mosharraf were grievous in nature but the injuries do not come within the definition of grievous injuries as provided in section 320 of the Penal Code and accordingly, the order of conviction under section 326 of the Penal Code passed against this accused is liable to be set aside. He further argued that the accused-petitioner Mojlem Akond has been convicted under section 326 of the Penal Code for causing injuries to PW 3 Abdus Salam but the injuries on the person of victim Abdus Salam do not come within the mischief of section 320 of the Penal Code and, as such, order of conviction and sentence is also liable to be set aside. He then argued that the witnesses examined in this case are closely related to each other excepting PW 5 a seizure list witness and there is also allegation of previous enmity between the parties and the witnesses are highly interested persons and no independent and disinterested witnesses were examined in this case. He next argued that there has been inordinate delay in lodging the First Information Report and this makes the prosecution case rather doubtful. He lastly, argued that the major portion of the prosecution case that the accused-petitioners and others being armed with deadly weapons attacked the house of the informant and also looted away 10 maunds of rice, golden chain, cloth, etc. worth Taka 43,000.00 has not been proved and both the courts below disbelieved this part of the prosecution case. 

 6. The learned Advocate for the petitioners then argued that when the major part of the prosecution case has not been proved the remaining part of the prosecution case ought to have been disbelieved by the trial Court and the court of appeal below. In support of his contention he has placed the case of Gays Din and others vs. Emperor, reported in AIR 1934 (Oudh.) 124. In my opinion, the facts of that case are distinguishable from the present case and that case has no manner of application in the present case because in that case the learned Counsel for the Crown finally urged that even if the charge under sections 332/147 IPC could not be legally sustained upon the evidence on the record the accused might at least be convicted of the offences of causing simple hurt and of riot. In that case it was observed that, where the major portion of the prosecution evidence is found to be false and tainted with gross exaggeration it is impossible to build up a case of an offence-under section 323 IPC out of the mass of lies told by the prosecution witnesses. 

 7. From the evidence on record it appears that the accused-petitioner Moslem Ali @ Moslem Mollah @ Fattah Mollah was charged under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code as under: 

 It is submitted that there is no evidence on record that on the order of the accused-petitioner Moslem Mollah @ Fattah Mollah any injury was caused to the informant Habibur Rahman PW 1 and, as such, the order of conviction and sentence of the accused-petitioner under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code is illegal and cannot be sustained. 

 8. Mr. MA Hafiz, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the State, submitted that it is true that charge was framed against the accused-petitioner Moslem Mollah @ Fattah Mollah under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code on the allegation that he gave order to kill the informant Habibur Rahman and he submitted that this defect is curable under section 537 of the CrPC but he could not show any decision in support of his contention. A charge is an important step in a criminal proceeding and the accused is answerable to the charges levelled against him. The object of framing charge is to ensure that the accused may have as full particulars as are possible of the accusation brought against him. In my opinion this defect is not curable under section 537 of the CrPC and there is no evidence on record against the accused-petitioner for offence under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code. Section 114 of the Penal Code refers to the case where a person prior to the commission of the offence renders himself liable as an abettor is present when the offence is committed. Since there is no evidence against the accused-petitioner, Moslem Mollah@ Fattah Mollah that at his order any injury was caused to the informant Habibur Rahman, in my opinion the courts below were not justified in convicting him under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code and sentencing him thereunder Moreover, in our country it is a common tendency to implicate the elder member of the family as hukum giver. Accordingly, the order of conviction and sentence passed upon the accused-petitioner Moslem Mollah @ Fattah Mollah under sections 326/114 of the Penal Code is liable to be set aside. 

 10. Accused-petitioner Ayub Ali was convicted under section 326 of the Penal Code and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3 years and to pay a fine of Taka 500.00 in default, to suffer, simple imprisonment for 6 months more for causing grievous injuries to witness Mosharraf Hossain by giving dao blow on the head. Accused Mojlem Akond was also convicted under section 326 of the Penal Code and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 3 years and to pay a fine of Taka 500.00 in default, to suffer simple imprisonment for 6 months for causing grievous injuries to witness Abdus Salam. The medical officer PW 8 in his evidence stated that injuries on the person of victim Mosharraf Hossain and Abdus Salam are grievous in nature. The learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the courts below convicted the petitioners in the absence of any evidence which may come within the mischief of section 320 of the Penal Code and, as such, the order of conviction under section 326 of the Penal Code against the accused-petitioners 2-4 is bad in law and, as such, liable to be set aside. He further argued that although as per medical report the injuries on the person of victims Mosharraf Hossain and Abdus Salam are grievous in nature these cannot be termed as grievous injuries because these injuries do not come within the mischief of section 320 of the Penal Code. The learned Assistant Attorney-General also conceded to this position and accordingly, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the order of conviction and sentence against the accused-petitioner Ayub Ali and Mojlem Akond under section 326 of the Penal Code is liable to be set aside. He also submits that the accused-petitioners may be convicted under section 324 of the Penal Code if the prosecution case is believed. Mr. MA Hafiz, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, also conceded this legal position. 

 12. Mr. MA Hafiz, the learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that there is no illegality in producing the medical certificate by the informant himself and this is not very much material for the purpose of the case as the medical officer himself deposed in the case. He further submits that the Doctor who issued the medical certificate was examined in the trial Court and in his evidence he stated that he examined the victims for their injuries and issued certificate accordingly. 

 13. Mr. Khan Mahbub Hossain next argued that in revisional application under section 439 of the CrPC jurisdiction of the High Court is indeed wide and is not confined merely to errors of law. In the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction the High Court can even, in appropriate cases, disturb findings of fact, as for example, where the subordinate court has wrongly placed the onus of proof or not applied the correct principles relating to the appraisement of evidence or an important piece of evidence has been ignored. In support of his contention he has placed the case of Muhammad Samimullah Khan and another vs. State, reported in 15 DLR (SC) 150. He also cited the case of Kashem Ali vs. State, reported in 1989 BLD (AD) 13.
